sentences.text: Criminal Case/241/2003 on 24 May, 2016

Order  ON CHARGE:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The complaint had been filed against eight accused persons.
The sample of 'Besan' was lifted from M/s.
The Hans Plaza, a unit of accused no. 2 Hotel Hans Pvt. Ltd. Accused no. 1 (since declared Proclaimed Offender) was the vendor from whom the sample was purchased.
Accused no. 3 to 5 are stated to the directors of the accused no. 2 company.
Accused no. 6 is stated to be the supplier of the product to the accused no. 2.
Accused no. 8 is the firm that had manufactured/packed the product and accused no. 7 is its nominee.

2. As per the complaint, on 11.05.2001, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Usha Kiran and Suniti Kumar Gupta under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. S.
M. Haider reached along with their staff at M/s.
The Hans Plaza at 15, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi, where the accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles which were lying stored for use in sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Besan from the vendor, lying in sealed polypacks bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI,
panchnama, etc.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 30.05.2001, the PA found the sample to be adulterated because of presence of excreta and also because it contained khesari which should not be present as an admixture.

Upon receipt of report,
the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 26.06.2003 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (h), (l)
and (f) of PFA Act read with Rule 44-A of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre- summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 26.06.2003.

The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from the Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 25.08.2003, opining the sample to be not conforming to standards of besan due to presence of kesari dal starch and sample having tested positive for BOAA.

1 4.
After receiving the CFL report, vide order dated 21.12.2009, the court ordered that the case be tried as a warrant triable case.
The matter was thus listed for pre- charge evidence.
In pre-charge stage of evidence, the complainant examined PW-1 FI Bal Mukund and PW-2 FI Usha Kiran.
PW-2 was the part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

She deposed about the proceedings conducted by her on 11.05.2001 and narrated the steps undertaken by her during the sample proceedings, including disclosing identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1 kg of Besan, mixing/homogenizing it, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, fastening, sealing and marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor.

She also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-2/A, Notice as per Form- VI Ex. PW-1/B2 and Panchnama Ex. PW-2/B.
Vendor had handed over a copy of the bill showing purchase of commodity from accused no. 6.

On the next working day,
one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-2/D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-2/E.
PA report Ex. PW- 2/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-2.
She sent letters to vendor, supplier and manufacturer and received their replies.
Thereafter, sanction Ex. PW-1/A was taken from the Director PFA by PW-1 and the complaint Ex. PW-1/B was filed in the court.
Intimation Letter Ex.
PW-1/C along with copy of PA report was sent to the accused persons.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by respective Ld. Counsel for the accused persons wherein they denied that the samples were not representative or that the accused persons have falsely implicated.

5. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against all the accused persons sufficient to frame charge, on the ground that at this stage, the court cannot ignore the findings in the CFL report dated 25.08.2003 which as per section 13(3) and (5) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that both the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
6. On the other hand, respective Ld. Defence Counsel for accused persons have submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly.
Ld. Counsel have contended that there is huge variation in the reports of the PA and CFL, in as much as no excreta was found by the CFL, which was found to be upto nine pieces by the PA.

It is then pointed out that no percentage of kesari dal has been given by the CFL, arguing that it was negligible and presence of only traces of such kesari dal would not be an offence as it cannot be called as an 'admixture'.
7.
I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.

8. Since the matter has been ordered to be tried as a warrant triable case, as per section 245 and 246 CrPC, a charge can be framed against an accused in such warrant triable complaint cases if the evidence on record is sufficient to warrant his conviction if the same remains unrebutted.
9. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.

Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are Criminal Case/241/2003 on 24 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/159010139/
2 concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

10. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
11.

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
12. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296], Raja Ram Seth & Sons v. Delhi Administration [2012(2) FAC 523], State v. Sunil Dutt [2011(4)
JCC 2377] and State v. Rama Rattan Malhotra [2012(2) FAC 398].

sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

13. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.
14.
Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.
If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative, he would get benefit on that count.

3 15.

The commodity in the present case is Besan, which falls in Item no. A.18.04 of Appendix-B of PFA Rules, which lays down that Besan means a product obtained by grinding dehusked Bengal gram (Cicer arietinum).

The alleged violation in the present case is that of Rule 44-A of PFA Rules which prohibits sale, possession or use as ingredient in the preparation of any article of food intended for sale, Kesari gram, Kesari dal or Kesari dal flour and their mixtures with Bengal-gram.
16. In the case at hand, the report given by the PA has been partially nullified by the CFL as it never detected the presence of excreta, which was detected by the PA up to 9 pieces.
In view of above position, the PA report cannot now be looked into having been superseded by CFL report and the court has to confine itself only to the findings of CFL report.
17. The CFL found presence of Kesari dal/gram/flour in the sample due to the same having been tested positive in BOAA (Beta-N-Oxalyl L amino alkaline unusual amino acid) test.
However, what is important to note is, that no percentage or quantity or extent of such presence has been mentioned in the report.
In the absence of any such finding, the court cannot ascertain as to if the sample can be said to be a 'mixture' of kesari dal/gram/flour or not.

18. Rule 44-A, PFA Rules read as:
"No person ... shall ... sell or offer or expose for sale, or have in his possession for the purpose of sale, under any description or for use as an ingredient in the preparation of any article of food intended for sale- (a) Kesari gram (Lathyrus sativus) and its products,
(b) Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) and its products,
(c) Kesari dal flour (Lathyrus sativus) and its products,
(d) a mixture of Kesari gram (Lathyrus sativus) and Bengal-gram (Cicer arietinum) or any other gram,
(e) a mixture of Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) and Bengal-gram dal (Cicer arietinum)
or any other dal,
(f) a mixture of Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) flour and Bengal-gram dal (Cicer arietinum) flour or any other flour."
19.
Thus, the use of Kesari gram, Kesari dal and Kesari dal flour as such is totally prohibited for use.
However, only their 'mixtures' with Bengal-gram, Bengal-gram dal and Bengal-gram dal flour are prohibited for use as an ingredient in the preparation of any food article for sale.
20. It is pertinent to note that the commodity in this case was Besan (Bengal-gram or Cicer arietinum).
As such, this product has to fall in either of the clauses (d), (e) or (f) of Rule 44-A.

For Criminal Case/241/2003 on 24 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/159010139/
4 these three clauses to apply, it is necessary that to constitute a violation, there has to be a 'mixture'
of Kesari dal / gram / flour with Bengal-gram / dal / flour.
Had it been some product other than Bengal-gram / dal / flour, then the matter would have come under clauses (a), (b) or (c) of Rule 44-A and mere presence of kesari dal would have been a violation.

But in the case of Besan/Bengal-gram, the complainant is required to establish that it was a mixture with kesari dal /
gram / flour.

21. In the absence of any percentage or quantity having been mentioned in the report of CFL, it cannot be ascertained if the sample was a mixture of kesari dal with Bengal-gram or if kesari dal was present only in traces and negligible quantities.
If the presence of kesari dal is only in negligible quantities, that would not fall within the purview of 'mixture' and accused would be entitled to benefit therefrom.

Reliance can be safely placed on the judgements titled as Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Modern Flour Mills and General Industries [1984(II) PFA Cases 144] and Nagar Palika Parishad Khilchipur v. Rajendra Kumar [1988(II) PFA Cases 3].

sentences.text: No material has been brought on record by the prosecution to arrive at any conclusion contrary to what has been laid down in these judgements.
22. In a warrant triable criminal complaint case, the matter has to be sufficient to convict an accused if it is considered unrebutted.
But in this case, even if the entire material is considered unrebutted and correct as it is, no conviction can be maintained in view of the above position.
23. In view of the above discussed circumstances, this court is of the view that the material even if unrebutted is not sufficient to secure conviction of accused persons.
Having said so, all the accused persons (except accused no. 1) stand discharged from the matter.

However, bail bonds of accused no. 3 to 7 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
24.
File be consigned to the record room.

The same shall revive upon apprehension of accused no. 1 who is PO.
